title: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification

fields.label: Label
fields.value: Early embryological categories seldom coincide with phylogenetic classification

fields.label: Statement
fields.value: Early embryological data, up to and well beyond segmentation, are a subject for physiological and physical investigation, and their categories (yolk content, chromosome form and number, radial, bilateral or spiral cleavage) will only seldom and accidentally coincide with the natural or phylogenetic classification of the systematist.

fields.label: Chapter
fields.value: Ch. IV: On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell

fields.label: Quotation
fields.value: But we have little right to expect, and in point of fact we shall very seldom and (as it were) only accidentally find, that these embryological categories coincide with the lines of “natural” or “phylogenetic” classification which have been arrived at by the systematic zoologist.

fields.label: Agent
fields.value: delphisci On Growth and Form claim extractor

fields.label: Assumptions
fields.value: D’Arcy Wentworth Thompson, On Growth and Form (1st ed., Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1917), Chapter IV, “On the Internal Form and Structure of the Cell”; topic “Embryology and classification”. Scope: early embryonic development of animals

fields.label: Assessment
fields.value: GPT-5.6 Sol on thompson1917-ch04-15: partially-resolvable, resolvability 0.60

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: The prediction maps naturally to phylogenetic signal and classification tests. Accepted trees are public, but embryological trait data require substantial compilation and cover only a subset of animal diversity.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Code yolk content, chromosome traits, and cleavage mode across animal species, then quantify their phylogenetic signal and classification accuracy against accepted phylogenies. Rare, weak, or convergence-prone correspondence supports the claim; strong clade-specific prediction refutes it.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Species sampling is concentrated in model organisms.

No single open database comprehensively codes early embryological traits.

Phylogenetic relatedness itself induces nonindependence.

fields.value:

analysis feasibility: 0.45
data existence: 0.6
data adequacy: 0.45
discriminating power: 0.7

fields.label: Finding
fields.value: A mutual-information test between early embryonic categories and an independent phylogeny is a direct reading of 'seldom and accidentally'. Trees and chromosome counts are public; cleavage and yolk still have to be assembled from monographs, so only a subset of taxa can be scored promptly. Using a molecular tree avoids the circularity of testing embryological groups against a classification built from those same groups.

fields.label: Proposed test in the assessment
fields.value: Proposed test with existing data: Cross-tabulate early embryonic categories, yolk amount, cleavage geometry and chromosome number, against clades on a molecular phylogeny, and measure how much taxonomic structure those categories recover. Rare, scattered agreement would support the claim; categories that recover major clades at high frequency would refute 'seldom and accidentally'.

fields.label: Evidence against
fields.value:
Cleavage mode and yolk class are not in a single open table and must be compiled.

Older classifications sometimes used the same embryological characters, so agreement can be partly by construction unless the tree is molecular.

The claim covers animals from segmentation onward, a wider span than any one compiled matrix.
